text:
For years, Jenkins was the quiet workhorse behind every merge we shipped. But quiet isn't the same as healthy. Our setup had grown into a tangle of plugins, hand-tuned agents and pipeline definitions that only a few people felt confident touching. Builds were slow, the bill kept climbing, and keeping the server running had become a job of its own.

So we decided to move our CI to GitHub Actions. Over three weeks, we migrated all 41 of our pipelines and rewrote each one as a workflow that lives next to the code it builds. The results beat our expectations. Build time dropped from 14 minutes to 6, so developers now get feedback in less than half the time. Our monthly CI bill fell from $900 to $410, which saves us almost $6,000 a year.

In this post, we'll explain why we decided to leave Jenkins and how we ran the migration without slowing development. We'll also cover what tripped us up along the way and what we'd do differently next time.
